hints: Look at the zero crossings of the top graph going upward at $0$ and $500\text{ }\mu\text{s}$ to read off the time period $T$ of the sound wave.
Use $v = f\lambda$ with $v = 330\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $f = 1/T$ to find the wavelength $\lambda$ in metres.
Compare the extra distance $0.165\text{ m}$ with your value of $\lambda$ to decide how many whole wavelengths of phase lag the second molecule has.
walkthrough: Read the period from the given $X$ against time graph. It starts at $0$ going positive, returns to $0$ going positive at $500\text{ }\mu\text{s}$, so $T = 500\text{ }\mu\text{s} = 5.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ s}$.
Calculate the wavelength using $\lambda = vT$. Substituting $v = 330\text{ m s}^{-1}$ gives $\lambda = 330 \times 5.0 \times 10^{-4} = 0.165\text{ m}$.
The second molecule is $0.165\text{ m}$ further from the source, so the extra path is $0.165/0.165 = 1$ wavelength.
A path difference of one wavelength gives a phase difference of $360^{\circ}$ or $2\pi\text{ rad}$, so the two molecules vibrate in phase.
In-phase means at the same time $t$ the displacement $X$ is the same, with the same $0$, peak at $125\text{ }\mu\text{s}$, zero at $250\text{ }\mu\text{s}$ pattern. This is option D.

A.explanation: This is shifted by a quarter period with maximum $X$ at $t=0$, which would need a path difference of $\lambda/4$, not $0.165\text{ m}$.

B.explanation: This starts at $X=0$ going negative, which is antiphase to the given wave and would need an odd half-integer number of wavelengths.

C.explanation: This is shifted by half a period with zero crossings at $125\text{ }\mu\text{s}$ and $375\text{ }\mu\text{s}$, which would need a path difference of $\lambda/2$.

D.explanation: This has the same phase as the original graph because $0.165\text{ m}$ equals one full wavelength, so the motion repeats exactly.
